query: Which material can be used for lightweight and superior comprehensive performance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A precipitation‐strengthened lightweight high‐entropy alloy (HEA), identified via high‐throughput experimental and simulation screening with an optimized composition incorporating lightweight and cost‐efficient elements, will exhibit a lower density while maintaining or exceeding the mechanical performance of conventional high-temperature alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-principal element alloy candidate produced with standard processing that does not yet display the desired precipitation-strengthened microstructure.
generation.intervention: Systematic adjustment of the alloy composition (leveraging high‐throughput synthesis) combined with post-processing heat treatments to induce fine, uniformly distributed precipitates.
generation.conditions: Ambient and application-relevant loading conditions (as well as elevated temperatures for high-temperature applications) that mirror standard operational environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The controlled formation of nanoscale precipitates and refined grain structures within the HEA matrix.
generation.mechanism: Optimized element addition reduces overall density while the induced precipitation structure enhances strength and ductility by impeding dislocation motion, achieving a superior balance of lightweight and comprehensive performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional alloys (e.g., Ni-based superalloys), the new alloy is expected to show a significant reduction in density (potentially in the 15–30% range) while achieving comparable or improved yield strength and mechanical toughness under both ambient and elevated temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional high-performance alloys that typically achieve high strength at the expense of increased density and often require trade-offs in ductility or thermal stability.
generation.boundary: The performance benefits are expected within a specific compositional window optimized via high‐throughput screening; outside this window or under processing conditions that fail to induce the targeted precipitate formation, the advantages may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in density reduction and mechanical property enhancement is uncertain and may vary with processing precision and compositional tolerance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEA samples with systematically varied compositions around the optimized design and apply the post-processing during controlled heat treatments to induce precipitation. Test these alloys under ambient and elevated temperature conditions in a series of mechanical (e.g., compression, hardness) and density measurements.
measurements: Density via Archimedes or X-ray computed tomography
Mechanical properties including yield strength and compressive strength
Microstructural analysis using TEM/SEM to quantify precipitate size and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized alloy compositions do not result in a decrease in density by at least 15% relative to the conventional baseline or fail to achieve equal or superior mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility) under the defined testing conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. In the last few decades, the development of nickel-based superalloys has allowed a steady increase in operating temperatures of jet turbine engines, which leads to enhanced engine performance and efficiency. However, nowadays the engine operating temperatures have reached around 80% of the melting points of the materials, [1] i.e. , almost reaching the upper limit of usability, making it impossible to further increase the operating temperature. Thus, it is urgently needed to develop new materials that can withstand higher operating temperatures to achieve better performance, higher engine efficiency, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

Among various potential candidates, such as ceramics, [3] intermetallic compounds, [6] and refractory metals, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [8] have drawn considerable attention in the past decade because of their very encouraging properties, for instance, high melting points, superior mechanical properties at both room temperature and elevated temperatures, [13] which makes RHEAs of great interest for high-temperature application. Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question about which material can achieve both lightweight and superior comprehensive performance.
